section_title: What kind of house does God promise to build for David?

versions.label: BSB
paragraphs: 8 Now then, you are to tell My servant David that this is what the LORD of Hosts says: I took you from the pasture, from following the flock, to be the ruler over My people Israel. 9 I have been with you wherever you have gone, and I have cut off all your enemies from before you. Now I will make for you a name like that of the greatest in the land. 10 And I will provide a place for My people Israel and will plant them so that they may dwell in a place of their own and be disturbed no more. No longer will the sons of wickedness oppress them as they did at the beginning 11 and have done since the day I appointed judges over My people Israel. I will give you rest from all your enemies. The LORD declares to you that He Himself will establish a house for you.

12 And when your days are fulfilled and you rest with your fathers, I will raise up your descendant after you, who will come from your own body, and I will establish his kingdom. 13 He will build a house for My Name, and I will establish the throne of his kingdom forever. 14 I will be his Father, and he will be My son. When he does wrong, I will discipline him with the rod of men and with the blows of the sons of men. 15 But My loving devotion will never be removed from him as I removed it from Saul, whom I removed from before you. 16 Your house and kingdom will endure forever before Me, and your throne will be established forever.” 17 So Nathan relayed to David all the words of this entire revelation.

context_lines: The LORD reminds David that He took him from caring for sheep and made him ruler of Israel. David’s rise has depended on God’s presence and help. The message also promises a settled place and rest for God’s people.

Then the meaning of house changes. David has proposed a building for God; God promises an enduring family and kingdom for David. A descendant will build a house for God’s name, and God will establish his throne.

The promise includes a father-and-son relationship and discipline when the royal son does wrong. It also distinguishes David’s house from Saul’s: God’s loving devotion will not be withdrawn in the same way. The message ends with the repeated assurance that David’s house, kingdom and throne will endure forever.
common_interpretation_lines: [Wesley](https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-the-second-book-of-samuel/), [Henry](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/2_samuel/7.htm) and the [USCCB Bible notes](https://bible.usccb.org/bible/2samuel/7) recognize Solomon’s place in the promise while looking beyond him to the lasting kingship of Christ. [1 Chronicles 22:9–10](https://biblehub.com/bsb/1_chronicles/22.htm) explicitly names Solomon as the son who will build the house and describes God as his Father. [1 Kings 8:20](https://biblehub.com/bsb/1_kings/8.htm) treats Solomon’s succession and temple building as God keeping His word.

[Wesley](https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-the-second-book-of-samuel/) applies the warning about wrongdoing to Solomon and other descendants who sin, while understanding the everlasting throne in relation to Christ. [Henry](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/2_samuel/7.htm) also insists that the wrongdoing cannot describe Christ Himself, and extends the lesson of fatherly correction to believers. These readings distinguish the sinless Messiah from the failings of those associated with the royal promise.
It is therefore possible to recognize real events in Solomon’s reign without making his lifetime the whole meaning of an everlasting kingdom. The promise reaches further than any one mortal king.
god_plan_lines: The New Testament makes the connection to Jesus directly. In [Luke 1:30–33](https://biblehub.com/bsb/luke/1.htm), the angel announces that God will give Jesus the throne of David and that His kingdom will never end. The enduring kingship promised here is part of the announcement of who Jesus is.

[Hebrews 1:1–5](https://biblehub.com/bsb/hebrews/1.htm) applies the promise of a Father-and-Son relationship to Christ as it explains His greatness above the angels. It uses that promise without assigning the royal descendants’ wrongdoing to Jesus.

In [Acts 2:29–36](https://biblehub.com/bsb/acts/2.htm), Peter connects God’s oath about David’s descendant with Jesus’ resurrection and exaltation. David died; Jesus has been raised and declared Lord and Christ. God’s answer to the limits of David’s reign is not merely another brief reign, but the living King whose kingdom endures.
